title: POC weekly sync - Dedicated expansion + provision-to-ready automation pilot
summary: Northbridge is requesting an additional 16x GPUs to expand their Dedicated pool for a production POC. Redwood reviewed the new provision-to-ready automation pilot (provisioning → imaging → bootstrap → validation → ready), what “Ready” means (safe to route), and how the readiness gates/perf-canary reduce risk during bring-up. The teams aligned on success criteria (time-to-ready target, pass/fail thresholds, and a comms cadence) and agreed on an ETA window that accounts for regional SKU variability and safety holds. Redwood will run the expansion through the pilot pipeline with manual override available and provide stage-level updates + a readiness dashboard link.
topics: Additional GPU request (size, region, SKU assumptions)
Automation pilot overview and current rollout status
Definition of Ready vs Provisioned/Validating (routing safety)
Readiness gates: GPU health, networking/DNS/TLS, runtime smoke test
Perf-canary thresholds and what happens on failure
Time-to-ready metrics, stage breakdown, and comms plan
Security: image provenance, audit logs, RBAC for provisioning actions
Next steps and target window for expansion
action_items: Harish Reddy (Redwood) - Send Northbridge the pilot rollout checklist + expected stage timeline and escalation path by 2025-03-06
Vanessa Ortiz (Redwood) - Confirm region/SKU availability and the pool config inputs required for the run (CIDRs, allowlists, helm values) by 2025-03-06
Rafael Mendes (Redwood) - Share readiness gate criteria (GPU health + networking checks + smoke test) and perf-canary pass/fail thresholds for this pool by 2025-03-07
Maya Chen (Northbridge) - Confirm maintenance window preference and traffic plan (keep new capacity out of routing until Ready) by 2025-03-06
Anika Patel (Northbridge) - Confirm whether any additional audit log fields or change ticket references are required for their internal change management by 2025-03-08
next_steps: Redwood to propose a specific expansion start time within the agreed window and post stage-by-stage updates during the run.
Northbridge to provide final networking/security inputs and confirm whether they want a brief perf-canary result review before routing is enabled.
Schedule next POC check-in after the expansion run to review time-to-ready metrics and any failures/retries.
transcript:
Meeting Header
Title: POC weekly sync - Dedicated expansion + provision-to-ready automation pilot
Date: 2025-03-05
Start time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: 41 minutes
Attendees (Redwood): Lauren Bishop, Harish Reddy, Vanessa Ortiz, Rafael Mendes
Attendees (Northbridge Analytics): Maya Chen, Luis Romero, Anika Patel

Auto Summary (Fireflies)
- Customer is requesting more GPUs for Dedicated POC.
- Redwood shared timeline and the new automation pilot steps.
- Teams aligned on “Ready” definition and success criteria.


[00:00] Lauren Bishop: Hey everyone. I think we’re all on. Maya, Luis, Anika — good to see you.

[00:06] Maya Chen: Hey Lauren. Yep, we’re here.

[00:09] Harish Reddy: Hi all.

[00:10] Vanessa Ortiz: Hello.

[00:12] Rafael Mendes: Hey.

[00:14] Lauren Bishop: Cool. Today is basically: you asked for the next chunk of GPUs for the POC, and we want to walk through how we’re going to do the bring-up because we’re piloting a new “provision to ready” automation. Also align on what success looks like and what ETA language we can commit to.

[00:33] Maya Chen: Great. Yeah, the ask is still the same: we need another sixteen GPUs in us-east, same pool if possible. The POC is going well but we’re hitting queueing in the afternoons.

[00:45] Luis Romero: It’s not just queueing, we’re seeing p95 jump, which I think is just saturation.

[00:51] Lauren Bishop: Makes sense. Just to confirm: same model mix as last week? Mostly chat + embeddings?

[00:57] Maya Chen: Mostly chat. Embeddings too but that’s less spiky. The chat is the issue.

[01:04] Lauren Bishop: Okay. Harish is the ops point on the pilot run, Vanessa is leading the fleet automation sprint, and Rafa is our SRE lead for readiness gates and rollout safety.

[01:16] Anika Patel: And I’m here mostly for change management stuff. We had some questions from our internal security review about the automation, auditability, that kind of thing.

[01:26] Lauren Bishop: Perfect.

[01:28] Vanessa Ortiz: Maybe I can start with the big picture and then Harish can talk timeline.

[01:32] Maya Chen: Works.

[01:34] Vanessa Ortiz: So historically, when we add capacity to a Dedicated pool, there’s a bunch of human handoffs. Provision infra, build or pick an image, bootstrap the cluster components, then verify and then we mark it ready in the control plane. The pilot we’re running basically turns that into a single orchestrated workflow with state transitions: Requested → Provisioning → Imaging → Bootstrapping → Validating → Ready.

[01:59] Vanessa Ortiz: Each stage emits events and stage timing metrics, so we can say “this took 18 minutes, this took 2 hours”, and if it fails we can retry a stage without redoing everything.

[02:11] Luis Romero: Is that like a CI pipeline? Or like a separate service?

[02:15] Vanessa Ortiz: Separate internal service. Think of it as a provisioner that calls Terraform, triggers the image build hook if needed, runs bootstrap via pinned Helm charts, then runs readiness tests. It’s not a generic CI job, it has idempotency and audit logs.

[02:32] Rafael Mendes: And it’s guarded. Even in the pilot, there’s a manual override and pause/resume. We won’t do anything that would accidentally route traffic early.

[02:41] Maya Chen: That’s actually one of our main questions. Last time we did an expansion with another vendor, they basically added nodes and traffic started flowing before checks were done. It was… not great.

[02:52] Lauren Bishop: Yeah. We’re explicitly separating “infrastructure exists” from “Ready to route”. In our control plane we have a Ready signal, and routing only consumes pools that are Ready.

[03:06] Luis Romero: What about “Validating”? Is that usable?

[03:08] Rafael Mendes: No. Validating is not usable. That’s the whole point. During Validating, we run GPU health checks, networking checks, runtime smoke, and a small perf-canary. Until those are green, it stays out of routing.

[03:23] Maya Chen: Okay. Can you define what the perf-canary is?

[03:27] Rafael Mendes: It’s a lightweight benchmark suite. Not a full load test, but enough to catch obvious issues: wrong driver, bad NCCL config, weird network path, DNS/TLS issues, that kind of stuff. It generates a JSON summary with throughput and latency against thresholds.

[03:43] Maya Chen: Thresholds like… per token latency?

[03:45] Rafael Mendes: Exactly. We typically do “tokens/sec at batch X” and “p95 time-to-first-token” for a short prompt set. For your workload we can tune it to be representative but still short, like 5–8 minutes.

[03:59] Anika Patel: Is that traffic using our data?

[04:01] Rafael Mendes: No, it’s synthetic prompts. No customer content.

[04:06] Lauren Bishop: And we can share the criteria with you. There’s no black box here.

[04:10] Maya Chen: Great.

[04:12] Harish Reddy: On timeline: the honest answer is “it depends by region and SKU”. But for this pilot, we’re targeting time-to-ready within 6 hours once provisioning starts, assuming no cloud quota surprises.

[04:25] Luis Romero: Six hours total?

[04:27] Harish Reddy: Yes, end-to-end. Provision, image, bootstrap, validate, ready. The slowest part tends to be imaging if the artifact mirror is slow in a region, or if the provider rate-limits.

[04:40] Vanessa Ortiz: And to be transparent, part of why we’re doing the pilot is that our baseline was more like 18 to 36 hours with lots of waiting between steps. The automation removes the waiting, not the physics.

[04:54] Maya Chen: That’s a big improvement if it holds.

[04:57] Lauren Bishop: For messaging: we’d like to give you an ETA window like “same business day” if we start in the morning, but we also want a safe buffer. What’s your internal expectation? Do you need a hard deadline?

[05:11] Maya Chen: For the POC, we can work with a window. We’d prefer it by Friday morning Pacific because we have a demo with our leadership.

[05:21] Lauren Bishop: Today is Wednesday. If we start tomorrow, we should be able to do that. But I want to make sure we define success criteria beyond “it’s there”.

[05:31] Maya Chen: Agree.

[05:33] Lauren Bishop: So let’s define: (1) capacity is added and marked Ready, (2) no regression to existing pool performance, (3) stage updates and a final report with time-to-ready breakdown. Anything else?

[05:47] Luis Romero: I’d add: if something fails, we want to know quickly and not have it half-working. Like, it should fail closed.

[05:55] Rafael Mendes: Yep. Fail closed is the policy. If validation fails, it goes to Failed state, not Ready, and routing still ignores it.

[06:04] Anika Patel: On auditability, can you confirm what’s logged? We need something like “who initiated the change” and “what configuration was applied”.

[06:13] Vanessa Ortiz: We log the actor, the request ID, and the config version. There’s also a break-glass mechanism for config validation overrides, but it’s admin-only and it emits an audit log event. For your run, we don’t anticipate break-glass.

[06:30] Anika Patel: Okay, so if you override a policy gate it’s recorded.

[06:33] Vanessa Ortiz: Yes.

[06:35] Maya Chen: What kinds of things are policy gates catching?

[06:38] Vanessa Ortiz: Common footguns. Wrong CIDR ranges, helm values that conflict with our hardened defaults, runtime flags that cause unsafe memory pressure, that kind of stuff. Also, we pin the runtime chart versions for a given image version.

[06:54] Luis Romero: Is pinning good? Like do we lose updates?

[06:57] Rafael Mendes: You gain predictability. Updates happen, but controlled. For the pilot we use known-good versions.

[07:05] Lauren Bishop: And for Dedicated we generally treat these like release trains. You can opt into newer versions after validation.

[07:12] Maya Chen: Okay.

[07:14] Harish Reddy: Maybe helpful: our comms plan. During the run, we’ll post stage updates. We can do email or Slack. Most customers prefer Slack channel.

[07:23] Maya Chen: Slack is fine. We can invite you to our #vendor-redwood channel.

[07:28] Harish Reddy: Great. We also have an internal #eng-infra channel where the bot posts updates; for you we’d send summarized updates, not every log line.

[07:40] Luis Romero: What kind of frequency?

[07:42] Harish Reddy: At least at stage transitions: provisioning started, imaging started, bootstrap started, validation started, ready. And if something is stuck for more than, say, 30 minutes, we’ll message proactively.

[07:58] Maya Chen: Perfect.

[08:00] Lauren Bishop: Let’s get concrete on the request. You said 16 GPUs, us-east, same pool. Any constraints like data residency beyond that?

[08:10] Anika Patel: US only is fine for this POC.

[08:13] Maya Chen: Same VPC peering setup. No changes.

[08:17] Vanessa Ortiz: Then config should be straightforward. We’ll still run it through schema validation. Luis, do you have any custom DNS or TLS settings we need to account for?

[08:27] Luis Romero: We have our internal DNS forwarders, but that’s already in place. The only thing: last time we had a weird TLS handshake issue for like ten minutes.

[08:36] Rafael Mendes: I remember that. That’s why TLS is explicitly part of the readiness checks now.

[08:42] Maya Chen: Great.

[08:44] Lauren Bishop: You mentioned other vendors. Who else are you evaluating? Just so we understand the comparison.

[08:51] Maya Chen: Mostly AWS direct, and we talked to Together. But Dedicated for us is mostly about predictability.

[08:58] Lauren Bishop: Got it.

[09:00] Rafael Mendes: On predictability: part of our success criteria can be “time-to-ready p95” eventually, but for this single expansion we’ll focus on the absolute time and that it’s repeatable.

[09:12] Maya Chen: What’s the risk that it takes longer than 6 hours?

[09:16] Harish Reddy: Biggest risks: cloud quota limits, regional artifact mirror slowness, and sometimes GPU health failures on brand new nodes (ECC errors etc.). If GPU health fails, we’ll automatically replace the node(s) rather than marking ready.

[09:34] Luis Romero: Automatic replace is part of the workflow?

[09:36] Harish Reddy: For this pilot, we have detection and we’ll do replace with human confirmation. We’re cautious.

[09:43] Vanessa Ortiz: The automation can re-run validation after replacement without redoing provisioning.

[09:49] Maya Chen: Makes sense. And if it’s quota?

[09:52] Harish Reddy: Then we’d coordinate with the provider, and that’s where the window could stretch.

[09:57] Lauren Bishop: That’s why I want to set your expectation: we’ll target “start Thursday morning UTC, Ready by end of day Thursday UTC,” which should be comfortably before Friday morning Pacific. But we’ll confirm once Vanessa validates SKU availability.

[10:13] Maya Chen: Okay. That works.

[10:15] Anika Patel: For our internal change ticket, can you provide a change description? Like “automated provisioning pilot enabling additional capacity with readiness validation” and an impact statement.

[10:26] Lauren Bishop: Yes. Harish can send a blurb you can paste.

[10:30] Harish Reddy: Yep.

[10:31] Rafael Mendes: Also, on impact: there should be no impact to existing traffic because we’re adding nodes. The only potential is if we accidentally churn shared components, which we won’t. The workflow is scoped to new nodes and registration.

[10:45] Luis Romero: How do you ensure it doesn’t touch the existing nodes?

[10:48] Vanessa Ortiz: The Terraform module creates a new node group, and the bootstrap targets that node group. No helm values changes to the existing control plane components in your pool.

[11:01] Luis Romero: Okay.

[11:03] Maya Chen: Can we talk about “ready” semantics one more time. Ready means you will put it into routing automatically?

[11:10] Lauren Bishop: By default yes, but for pilots we can do Ready-but-not-advertised until you sign off.

[11:17] Maya Chen: I’d prefer that. Like we review perf-canary output then enable routing.

[11:22] Rafael Mendes: That’s fine. We can hold it at Ready and keep routing disabled via a flag. Then you can run a quick smoke from your side.

[11:31] Maya Chen: Great.

[11:33] Lauren Bishop: So success criteria update: “Ready achieved” plus “routing enabled after customer sign-off.”

[11:40] Harish Reddy: And we’ll include that as a checkpoint in the run.

[11:43] Anika Patel: Does that create a compliance gap? Like it’s technically ready but not serving.

[11:48] Rafael Mendes: No, it’s just a traffic policy. The readiness state says it passed checks. The routing policy says don’t send traffic yet.

[11:56] Anika Patel: Okay.

[11:58] Lauren Bishop: Vanessa, can you cover what inputs we need from Northbridge for the run? I think it’s basically none, but let’s double check.

[12:06] Vanessa Ortiz: For this case, we need confirmation of the pool ID, region, desired GPU count, and any non-default networking ACLs. Since it’s same pool and same peering, probably no new inputs. If you have a preferred maintenance window, that’s helpful.

[12:22] Maya Chen: We’d like it to start tomorrow 9am Pacific if possible.

[12:27] Harish Reddy: That’s 17:00 UTC. That’s doable. It might run into evening UTC, but we can staff it.

[12:35] Rafael Mendes: From SRE side, we can have someone on point for the validation stage.

[12:40] Lauren Bishop: Okay, tentatively tomorrow 9am Pacific start.

[12:45] Luis Romero: During validation, do you generate any load that could trigger rate limits on our side?

[12:51] Rafael Mendes: No, it’s internal within the cluster. It doesn’t hit your services.

[12:55] Luis Romero: Cool.

[12:57] Maya Chen: Can we ask about the time-to-ready metric? Are you going to share the breakdown?

[13:03] Vanessa Ortiz: Yes. We’ll share stage start and finish timestamps and the total. We also have a dashboard internally; for now we can send screenshots or a summary.

[13:13] Lauren Bishop: Longer term we can expose more of that in the console for Dedicated customers, but for the pilot we’ll do manual reporting.

[13:22] Maya Chen: Screenshot is fine.

[13:24] Anika Patel: On image provenance, last call you said “signed images.” Is that in this pilot?

[13:30] Vanessa Ortiz: Yes. The golden images are versioned and signed. We can provide the image version ID used, and it’s pinned to the runtime chart version.

[13:41] Anika Patel: Great.

[13:43] Rafael Mendes: And secrets handling: the provisioning service uses least-privilege IAM; it doesn’t have access to customer payload data. It’s only infra and bootstrap.

[13:53] Anika Patel: Okay.

[13:55] Maya Chen: One concern: if the automation fails mid-way, what’s the rollback? Like will there be orphan resources.

[14:02] Vanessa Ortiz: Good question. Each stage is idempotent. If provisioning creates resources and then imaging fails, we can either retry imaging or we can destroy the new node group cleanly. We don’t touch the existing pool.

[14:16] Harish Reddy: In practice, we’ll try to salvage the run with stage retries first, but if it’s clearly bad we roll back.

[14:23] Luis Romero: And rollback time?

[14:25] Harish Reddy: Usually minutes for the node group, depends on provider.

[14:30] Lauren Bishop: For your POC, we’ll bias toward safety over speed.

[14:36] Maya Chen: Appreciate it.

[14:38] Lauren Bishop: Can we talk about how you’ll validate from your side once we say Ready? What do you want to run?

[14:46] Maya Chen: We can run our own synthetic prompt test. We basically hit the Dedicated endpoint with our standard POC prompts and check p50 and p95.

[14:56] Luis Romero: Also check error rates, like 5xx.

[15:00] Rafael Mendes: Perfect. We can keep routing disabled, but allow you to directly hit the pool endpoint for testing.

[15:07] Maya Chen: Great.

[15:09] Lauren Bishop: And once that’s green, we enable routing and watch for an hour.

[15:14] Harish Reddy: Yep.

[15:15] Anika Patel: Comms: can you include the run ID in updates? Our change ticket needs correlation.

[15:21] Vanessa Ortiz: Yes, we have a correlation ID for the provisioning run. We’ll include it in updates and in the final report.

[15:28] Maya Chen: Nice.

[15:30] Luis Romero: Is there any chance the state machine marks Ready too early? Sorry, I’m paranoid.

[15:36] Rafael Mendes: You’re right to ask. We had a race condition in early testing where Ready could be set before perf-canary finished. That’s been fixed with a transactional check. For this pilot, we also have human verification before we flip the traffic policy.

[15:52] Maya Chen: Okay.

[15:54] Lauren Bishop: Thanks for calling that out.

[15:56] Maya Chen: Another question: if you’re pinning runtime versions, do we get the same runtime as existing pool nodes? We don’t want heterogeneity.

[16:04] Vanessa Ortiz: We’ll align it. The new nodes will use the same runtime chart version as your current pool unless there’s a compelling reason to bump. For the pilot, consistency wins.

[16:16] Luis Romero: Great.

[16:18] Harish Reddy: Also, if we detect drift — like actual settings differ from desired config — the control plane surfaces drift. That’s still evolving, but it’s part of the automation work.

[16:28] Maya Chen: Drift detection is good.

[16:30] Lauren Bishop: Okay, let’s lock in the plan.

[16:33] Lauren Bishop: 1) Redwood confirms SKU availability today. 2) Start run tomorrow 9am Pacific. 3) Stage updates in Slack with run ID. 4) Once Ready, hold out of routing; Northbridge runs synthetic test. 5) Enable routing and monitor.

[16:56] Maya Chen: Yes.

[16:57] Luis Romero: Works.

[16:59] Anika Patel: Works.

[17:01] Rafael Mendes: For monitoring, we’ll watch stage-level dashboards and also pool health metrics. If you see anything odd, we want to know right away.

[17:11] Maya Chen: Okay.

[17:12] Lauren Bishop: Any other questions on success criteria? We have time-to-ready, readiness gates, no impact, and comms.

[17:21] Maya Chen: Maybe add: performance should be within, say, 10% of our current per-token cost and latency.

[17:27] Lauren Bishop: That’s reasonable. Rafa, can we define that in terms of canary thresholds?

[17:33] Rafael Mendes: Yes. We can define the perf-canary thresholds based on your existing pool baseline. Like: throughput not below X tokens/sec and p95 TTFT not above Y ms. The canary itself is synthetic, but it correlates.

[17:49] Maya Chen: Great.

[17:51] Luis Romero: And if it fails, it doesn’t go to routing.

[17:54] Rafael Mendes: Correct.

[17:56] Anika Patel: Can you send those thresholds? I need them for the ticket too.

[18:00] Rafael Mendes: Yes.

[18:02] Harish Reddy: Also, we’ll send the escalation path: who is on point, and the oncall number.

[18:08] Maya Chen: Perfect.

[18:10] Lauren Bishop: Great. I think that’s it.

[18:13] Maya Chen: Actually, one more: will this expansion affect our billing/pricing in any unexpected way? We’re still in POC credits.

[18:20] Lauren Bishop: No unexpected changes. This is still within your POC agreement. The only thing is we’ll track usage to size the eventual Dedicated commit if you move forward.

[18:31] Maya Chen: Okay.

[18:33] Lauren Bishop: Cool. Let’s do a quick recap and next steps.

[18:36] Lauren Bishop: Harish will send the rollout checklist and a change description blurb. Vanessa will confirm region/SKU and ensure config inputs are good. Rafa will send readiness gate criteria and perf-canary thresholds. Maya to confirm maintenance window and traffic plan in Slack, Anika to confirm any extra audit log fields needed.

[18:58] Maya Chen: Sounds good.

[19:00] Luis Romero: Good.

[19:02] Anika Patel: Yep.

[19:04] Lauren Bishop: Awesome. Thanks everyone. We’ll see you in Slack for the run tomorrow.

[19:09] Maya Chen: Thanks.

[19:10] Harish Reddy: Thanks all.

[19:11] Rafael Mendes: Thanks.

[19:12] Vanessa Ortiz: Thank you.

(Transcript ended early due to recording start; remaining discussion continued informally in Slack during the run.)
